knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE)
```


Even if it is not part of the `{tidyverse}`, the package `{janitor}` is a great
companion as is features many functions to clean and quickly explore the data.

```{r ,echo = FALSE, fig.cap='The package `{janitor}` cleans your data', fig.align='center', out.width = "30%"}
  knitr::include_graphics("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sfirke/janitor/main/man/figures/logo_small.png")
```
As usual, you can _attach_ the package `{janitor}` with a call to `library()`

```{r}
library(janitor)
```

And for our examples, we'll be (again) using the `wta_grand_slam_data.csv` dataset,
with some modifications: 

```{r}
```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
library(lubridate)

wta_data <-
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/gruggeri/tennis_wta/master/wta_grand_slam_data.csv" %>% 
  read_csv(
    col_types = cols(.default = "c")
    ) %>% 
  mutate(
    year = as.numeric(year),
    tourney_date = ymd(tourney_date))
```



# Frequency tables



`{janitor}` features a very useful function called `{tabyl}`. The purpose of the  
function is to create quick-and-dirty _frequency tables_ by counting
the number of occurrences of a certain value in a variable. For instance
the variable `winner_hand` in our polished dataset `wta_data` contains 
information on whether the winner is right-handed, left-handed or uses both hands. 

To compute the amount of matches won by each of these categories of players, we 
can use the function `tabyl()` as follows:

```{r}
wta_data %>% 
  tabyl(winner_hand)
```
We can see that most of the matches are won by right-handed players. For the moment
the display is a bit raw, but we'll get improve it in the following sections

# Cross-tabulation

We could be interested in producing cross-tabulations, i.e. count the ocurrences 
of the crossing between two variables. This can easily be done in `tabyl()` by adding
a second variable to the call. 

Suppose we want to count the amount of winning matches by hand in each of the 
tournaments, all we need to do is to add the tournament as another variable, 
we can do that by adding `winner_hand` in our call to `tabyl()`

```{r}
wta_data %>% 
  tabyl(tourney_name, winner_hand)
```

# Formatting

There are ways to improve the display of these tabulations, one of them consists
in adding the functions prefixed by `adorn_`. For instance, if we want to 
improve the display of the percentages in a frequency table we can use the 
function `adorn_pct_formatting`, which multiplies the "percentage" columns by 
100 and adds the percentage sign `%` when the argument `affix_sign` is set to 
`TRUE` (the default)

```{r}
wta_data %>% 
  tabyl(winner_hand) %>% 
  adorn_pct_formatting(digits = 2, affix_sign = TRUE)
```

Crosstabs can also be modified to show totals either in the columns, rows or in 
both dimensions using the function `adorn_totals()` which features the argument 
`where`. For instance, setting it to `where="col"` adds a column with the sum 
for the columns. 
```{r}
wta_data %>% 
  tabyl(winner_hand, tourney_name) %>% 
  adorn_totals(where = "col")
```
In a similar manner, setting `where = c("col", "row")` computes totals in both 
the row and column dimensions. 
```{r}
wta_data %>% 
  tabyl(winner_hand, tourney_name) %>% 
  adorn_totals(where = c("col", "row"))
```

To compute the percentages, we use `adorn_percentages()` and set the `denominator`
argument to either `"row"` or `"col"`. Just like we did for the frequency table, 
we can format the display of this percentage with the function 
`adorn_pct_formatting()`
```{r}
wta_data %>% 
  tabyl(winner_hand, tourney_name) %>% 
  adorn_percentages(denominator = "row") %>% 
  adorn_pct_formatting(digits = 2, affix_sign = TRUE)
```

Finally, were we to want to display either of these tables in a document, we could add a title 
with `adorn_title()` and render it nicely with `knitr::kable()`

```{r}
wta_data %>% 
  tabyl(winner_hand) %>% 
  adorn_pct_formatting(digits = 2, affix_sign = TRUE) %>%
  adorn_title(row_name = "Winner hand",
              col_name = "Percentages of won matches by used hand") %>% 
  knitr::kable()
```

# `clean_names()`

The package `{janitor}` features a very nice function that we haven't used until 
now. In this bonus section, we will explore the use of `clean_names()`

Very often the column names of the imported dataset won't have a very convenient 
format. For example, column names can contain spaces, special symbols such as 
`(`, etc. 

Let's illustrate this with a makeshift dataset called `team_bad_names`

```{r}
team_bad_names <- read_csv("data/team_bad_names.csv")
names(team_bad_names)
```

In this case, it is not very convenient to refer to these columns, 
and one has to wrap column names into a pair of `` ` `` (backticks): 
For instance, in order to select a variable using our `{dplyr}` verb `select()`, 
we'd have to proceed as follows:
```{r}
team_bad_names %>% select(`First Name`)
```

Fortunately, we do not have to worry about that because we have an extremely 
useful function `clean_names()` from the `{janitor}` package. This function will 
remove spaces and all other special symbols and covert all letters to lower case. 

The argument of this function is the tibble, so that we 
can pass an imported tibble directly into it. As usual, before using a function 
from a package, we need to load the package first. 
```{r}
library(janitor)
team_bad_names <- read_csv("data/team_bad_names.csv") %>% clean_names()
team_bad_names %>% names()
```

```{r}
team_bad_names %>% select(first_name)
```
